title: What could ‘formidable’ Red Bull achieve after resurgence?
excerpt:
Just a few months ago, speculation was rife that Max Verstappen was exploring his options outside of Red Bull as they struggled to adapt to the sport's new regulations – but now, they’ve become one of the biggest threats on the grid.

After Red Bull lost ground to Mercedes, Ferrari and McLaren, the Dutchman was convinced to extend his contract to 2030 and remain with the team that previously helped him secure four Drivers’ Championships.

Their upgrades have seen them take a remarkable step forward, enabling Verstappen to win in Malaysia and Singapore and bring him into contention for a P2 finish in the standings.

The resurgence would’ve been hard to predict at the start of the season – Red Bull scored just 16 points in the opening three rounds – so Jolyon Palmer and Alex Jacques dissected just how impressive the progress has been on the latest episode of official podcast F1 Nation, presented by AWS – Global AI partner of Formula 1.

“I look at the Red Bull with the upgrades and the weaknesses that we used to hear don't seem to be there,” Palmer said. “They're good at kerb riding.

“I think Max mentioned the downshifts once in Singapore, because he starts to feel the instability as he's banging down the gears, but they've been able to dial that out for years anyway. Right now, I don't see a weakness in it.”

Elaborating on Verstappen’s performances, Jacques added: “He had a car that didn't unlock the entire potential of his difference-making driving ability, which is that super sensitive front end that a hatful of very talented drivers in the second Red Bull car couldn't live with.

“Ironically, it's an update at the rear of the car that's unlocked the overall balance. And now suddenly you have Max with total confidence, with the machine that is working entirely to his liking.

“He's finished a tenth away in Baku, he's rattled off everything he can win since, and [has] super high confidence for a driver who was mulling whether it was worth staying with the team in recent times.”

Red Bull’s transformation could be compared to the one that McLaren enjoyed en route to their title-winning seasons in 2024 and 2025, but Palmer argued that the Milton Keynes-based outfit have overcome even greater obstacles.

“When you look at the whole picture here, the uptrend for Red Bull is massive,” the former Renault F1 driver explained. “We've spoken for years about McLaren’s turnaround in form a couple of years ago. It was huge when Lando [Norris] came from being nowhere, to suddenly we were thinking, ‘can he fight for a championship?’ before he did.

“But I think this Red Bull turnaround in form might be on paper, when you look at the percentage difference, I think it's got to be the biggest, if they can cement it through these final races. After six races, he was 113 points behind Kimi Antonelli. In the 11 races since, he's lost six points to Kimi. If you started the championship after Monaco, Max will be champion.

“That's the incredible form that he showed when he didn't have the fastest car and now he does. He's formidable and I think he's got everyone else almost fearing the battle with him. There's almost a sense of resignation when you take on Max from the rest of the field.”

Verstappen’s commitment to Red Bull was partly influenced by his strong relationship with Team Principal Laurent Mekies, who recently signed a contract extension that lasts through the 2031 season.

Reflecting on the Frenchman’s leadership, Palmer said: “I think he's been remarkable. What a hire to replace such a big character as Christian Horner. It felt like it was a poisoned chalice when he took over because the ship was sinking, wasn't it?

“It seemed like things were looking difficult. They throw Laurent into the mix and you think, ‘oh, he has got a big job, some high-profile names going, Max disgruntled, team falling away...’

“But he managed to galvanise them so well last season and even this year sort of just trying to get the ball moving again. And he's managed to keep the team with the full focus on winning races this season, when it could have really spiralled out of control early on. So I think Laurent has done a superb job and, looking forward to next year, you’ve got stability there.

“The powertrains department, what a superb job they've done. You don't even need to give Max the best car for him to be champion, I don't think. If he has a fighting chance, I think he'll start the [2027] season as favourite and the way that the team galvanised behind him – Isack Hadjar, we're not going to be thinking he can be champion – and I think that probably does help Max.

“The single-mindedness that Red Bull still have, post-Christian Horner, with Laurent coming in the team, gelling immediately with Max, I think that is still a key thing for the Drivers’ Championship.”

How Mekies has already made his mark at Red Bull

“I think what's interesting about Laurent is, I remember when he gave his first remarks, that the first thing he said to the personnel there was ‘what a race team this is’,” Jacques summarised. “He almost had to remind them of their capabilities and their stature in the sport as one of the most successful teams in recent times.

“So there was an element of the psychology of where that team was. All the headlines had been negative for a really long time. Then he had to make sure that the people that were replacing the big characters were up to it – they've all done very well.

“Then he had to make sure that Verstappen committed long-term, because if there was a brain drain before, the moment Max walks out on that team would have been an exodus. He did all of those. He thoroughly deserves his contract extension.”

Red Bull and Verstappen’s momentum was just one of the talking points that emerged in the United States Grand Prix preview, which saw Palmer and Jacques join F1 Nation host Tom Clarkson.

title: How Marcin Budkowski is shaping Cadillac’s next chapter
excerpt:
F1’s newest outfit underwent significant change in the summer as Marcin Budkowski took over from Graeme Lowdon as Cadillac Team Principal.

The 49-year-old’s experience in F1 is extensive. The long-time engineer has worked with multiple championship-winning teams, as well as governing body the FIA, and is the former Executive Director of Alpine. He’s also well versed in the media landscape having worked as a pundit with Eleven Sports Poland and Viaplay before landing his current gig.

With Cadillac’s next home race fast approaching in Austin, Budkowski sat down with F1.com to discuss how he’s settled into his role, what type of leader he’s going to be and why it’s important to build a winning culture as the squad embarks on the next phase of their journey.

‘We are definitely in action mode’

“It's been a bit of a whirlwind to be honest,” Budkowski tells me as we chat inside his office at the Sepang International Circuit. At this point it’s been just under two months since the Pole took charge of Cadillac.

His appointment came after CEO of the Cadillac F1 Team, Dan Towriss, decided the summer was the right time to “hand the baton off” to a new team principal, with Budkowski explaining at the time that he had a “number of exchanges” with Towriss amid interest from other F1 teams during his time away from the sport.

“I started the same day as the team was moving to the Silverstone facility,” Budkowski continues. “So, there was a feeling of novelty in the air from several sides, but it was great.

“It was super impressive for me also to work in this facility, because it's a really impressive and modern F1 standard facility. [I’ve been] getting to know people – quite a few people I knew from previous teams and previous experiences. [There’s] a lot of new faces, and then [I’ve been] progressively getting to meet everybody, speak to everybody and getting my head around how the team was structured and how it was operating – three days at the factory, four days at a track.”

As Budkowski reiterates consistently throughout our conversation, he’s been mightily impressed with what he’s seen so far given how new Cadillac are to the F1 world. Their approval to join the grid came in March 2025, meaning they had less than a full year to gear up for their debut campaign this season, so the progress has been monumental.

But there’s still been a price to pay given the rapidity with which they’ve had to work – Budkowski openly admits they’re seeing the consequences from some of the necessary shortcuts. That’s also why he listed listening and observing as one of his first priorities following his appointment, so he can get a full understanding of the situation before taking any next steps.

“It's not necessarily my first priority in terms of the team, but the logical thing to do is first to understand before you make any changes or take any actions,” he says. “I'm in this mixed phase now where I'm still meeting people, still having one-to-ones, still trying to spend time in the factory or in the garage talking to people to meet them and get feedback from within.

“But, at the same time, I'm already in a mode – and it's been a few weeks now – that I've identified a few things that I want to prioritise, a few things that I want to change or address and we're already working very hard on these things. In parallel, I still listen and absorb and [I’m] still being a sponge for information throughout the layers of the team. We are definitely in action mode, and we are prioritising and working hard on some of the areas that we need improving.”

Cadillac recruit technical leaders from Red Bull and Ferrari

A unique opportunity

Budkowski departed his role as Alpine Executive Director early in 2022 after four years with the squad and, in the time between then and now, he stayed active in the paddock courtesy of his media work with Eleven Sports Poland and Viaplay.

Becoming Cadillac F1 Team Principal is undoubtedly his biggest role to date, so what made this opportunity the right next chapter?

“I think it's a fantastic opportunity to be honest because it's a new team – even if it's already here racing for more than half a season,” he says. “It’s still in its building phase and, for me, having the opportunity to influence that, and to have an impact on how it's built, is very unique.

“It's not exactly the same as starting a team from the ground, but you still can have a lot more influence than within an established organisation. It's very ambitious, it's a great project, it is backed by TWG Motorsports and General Motors. It's got a very prestigious name in Cadillac. It's well-funded, but also our owners are all motorsport people.

“They love motorsport, they understand motorsport, they're winners, they want to win, they have a lot of ambition, but they're also realistic and understand the difficulty of the challenge, and that Formula 1 is like no other category in the world. We have 10 very competitive, very professional competitors on the grid that have taken years to get to where they are, and I think that mix of ambition, winning spirit and realistic approach was very important for me when I made the decision to join the project.”

‘There's the time for discussion and there's a time for action’

So, what type of person are Cadillac getting to lead them into their next phase as a Formula 1 team?

“Where to start?” Budkowski responds when I ask what kind of leader he is. “We talked about listening. I listen a lot, I approach things with an open mind – people and ideas and organisations.

“But I also like to act and like to move, so for me I'm very open. I'm listening, and I'm going to take all the views on board and try to get to the best possible solution for any problem. But then there's the time for discussion and there's a time for action.

“From the moment we make a decision, and we go for [it], I expect everybody to go strong. I'm very direct in my interactions, but I'm also very open. Trust and transparency are key in terms of building a cohesive management and team.

“But that's also why I like working for an American team. Americans are very direct and like action and that's how I am as well. I think, from that point of view, we get on really well with the owners and the leaders of this team as we see things very similarly.”

I'm very direct in my interactions, but I'm also very open.Marcin Budkowski, Cadillac Team Principal

What’s more, while Budkowski’s experience at various championship-winning outfits will undoubtedly prove useful in his quest to build Cadillac into a competitive operation, he also arguably has more media experience than any of the other team principals in the paddock.

After all, communication and clarity are key skills in a leadership role – something a media pundit needs to have in abundance when explaining what’s been happening on track to fans – and the Pole has learned a lot from his time working in that field.

“Also not to trip on your questions!” he laughs, highlighting another useful skill gained. “[Punditry] certainly allowed me to stay in the Formula 1 ecosystem, keep my networks and stay aware of what was going on in terms of the sport, because the sport is not as far from being only what's happening on the track.

“There's a lot of things happening in the background as well. There’s politics, there's interesting dynamics in the paddock that you have to understand.

“It did show me how F1 is perceived also by the outside world a bit better, because when you are in this job you spend so much time in the factory or the track and sometimes you miss that perspective, and I think that's a useful one.

“But yeah, the reality is, I think someone mentioned to me the other day... a less experienced journalist asked me, ‘how do you get from doing media to being team principal?’ Well, with all respect, I've done a few other things before my media time that probably account for a little bit more in terms of my ability to take this role than being a TV pundit!”

‘It's not about reinventing the wheel’

Budkowski’s debut in F1 came back in 2001 at Prost Grand Prix, the squad founded by four-time World Champion Alain, before spending six seasons with Ferrari. He then moved over to McLaren in 2007, working across both trackside and at the team’s headquarters, before rising to Head of Aerodynamics in 2012.

A move to the FIA followed, working across their technical and sporting divisions as well as taking on the role of Deputy Race Director, before Renault tempted him back to the team side ahead of their Alpine rebrand. Given his time with those outfits, he knows the core values needed to turn a team into one that can win.

“There's no magic formula, but being where we are in terms of the history of this team – the short history of the team and the competitiveness level – it would be foolish not to look at what works elsewhere in the best teams,” he explains.

Who is Cadillac's new Team Principal?

“It's not about reinventing the wheel. There are some principles that work pretty well and are visible in other teams.

"Equally, I think the culture and approach at Mercedes is different from the one at Red Bull, for example. Again, it will be different from the one at Ferrari, so there's no blueprint, and for that you have to build your own team culture and identity.

“It's also based on the people you have, but for me as a leader – listen and build trust. Transparency is very important to build a team with energy and action because, at the end of the day, there's a time for discussion and there's time for action.

“I'm someone who listens to all the inputs and takes every opinion into consideration. But at some point, you've got to make a decision, and from the moment you make a decision, I expect everybody to push in the same direction and I think that's very important.”

‘There are no shortcuts’

With Cadillac’s next phase underway as they gear up for their second home race of the season, their fans will understandably be keen to see where the journey goes from here. Budkowski, therefore, has a message for those invested in what’s to come.

“There are no shortcuts in modern F1,” he says. “There's just a lot of hard work – but the first thing is not about making good decisions, it's about avoiding bad decisions.

It's going to take time.Marcin Budkowski, Cadillac Team Principal

“There's a lot of truth in that, in terms of there's a lot of work in front of us and there's a lot of potential. My objective is to show progress in terms of track results – because that's what matters, the stopwatch and the results on the track – but also in the maturity of our organisation, the strength of the organisation and the factory as well as the operational excellence here at the track.

“Making the most every session, every weekend of the car we have, and that will set us on the path to go and progressively get to fight in the midfield and hopefully, at some point, build an organisation that's capable of fighting for podiums, for wins and for championships.

“But that's not the story of today. The story of today is to finish building a strong team and putting the right priorities in place and putting in the right trajectory. I think for the fans, for the people who support us, it's just to make sure [we show] that momentum, that progress, and show that vision to the front.

“It's going to take time. It's going to require some patience from our fans, but we have a lot of support already and I think we're excited to do that journey together with them, which is going to take time but it's hopefully going to deliver.”

He adds: “Sometimes it's difficult when you're in this job, you're so focused on the next step that you're [not here in the moment] sometimes [and] you have to stop for a second and realise that we're working in an incredible environment.

“But we're winners. Until we stand on that podium, we are not happy with ourselves and we want to continue pushing.”

title: Camara indicates the driver number he'd like to use in 2027
excerpt:
Following the announcement that Rafael Camara will replace Esteban Ocon at Haas from next season, the Brazilian has shared the driver number he is hoping to use when he makes his Formula 1 debut in 2027.

It was recently revealed that Camara would be promoted from Formula 2 – in which he currently leads the standings by seven points over Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov – to race for Haas next season.

That gives him the opportunity to choose his driver number, and like plenty before him, the 21-year-old has opted for one that has a personal link, although it won’t be confirmed until the official entry list is published by the FIA.

“I think we'll be using the number 50,” Camara said. “The first option would be five, but obviously Gabi [Gabriel Bortoleto] is using that.

“It's 50 because basically my birthday is 05/05/2005. I spoke with my dad and then he said it's 50, it makes sense with the birthday date, so I'll be using that one for next year.”

Haas aren't strangers to running #50 on their cars, with reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa having used it during FP1 sessions whilst Camara’s likely team mate Ollie Bearman did the same for his substitute appearances in 2024.

Camara went up against Hirakawa for Ocon’s seat in a Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) test at Portugal’s Autódromo Internacional do Algarve, where he impressed Team Principal Ayao Komatsu enough to be offered a full-time opportunity.

“It was a very intense two days,” he explained. “You knew that it was going to be important, the test, and you need to deliver in a way. You need to perform these two days with a new track, new car, and a new team.

“I just tried to learn everything and put it in place. There was also a huge amount of pressure, so I was really trying to focus, enjoy it, and make the most of the moment, and I think I was happy with the job I did in the end. I was happy with myself.

“I think I did the maximum I could, and whatever was the result, I was going to still be happy because it was the maximum I could [do]. I think when you’re yourself and you can do other things, you can do it. You can be pleased with that.

“I got a call from Ayao in Milan [about the seat], and then the first thing I said to him [was], ‘Are you sure?'. Obviously, I was very happy with that. Just super excited, and then I went to tell my parents – they also were staying – and I could tell them in person, [have a] good hug.

“I’m extremely happy, especially for my parents. There’s a lot of sacrifice on their side and making something that was a passion of a kid, and we are also not even from the motorsport world.

“We didn’t really know exactly what was the way to go to be here, so very proud of being here today, and I’m just enjoying the moment.”

title: Fornaroli set for McLaren FP1 runs after latest F1 test
excerpt:
Leonardo Fornaroli will return to the wheel of McLaren’s MCL40 over the coming weeks, with his next practice outings being planned for the Mexico City and São Paulo Grands Prix.

McLaren reserve driver Fornaroli made his first two FP1 appearances at the Barcelona-Catalunya and Hungary events earlier this season, meaning the young Italian will mark the team’s final two mandatory rookie sessions for 2026.

In preparation for those run-outs, Fornaroli – the 2024 F3 and 2025 F2 champion – joined McLaren’s Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) team at the Circuit Paul Ricard in France last weekend, where he completed almost 350 kilometres on the Grand Prix layout.

His sixth F1 test with the team, Fornaroli focused on longer runs (simulating FP1 sessions) and tried various set-ups aboard McLaren’s 2025 double championship-winning MCL39.

British racer Jake Hughes, who serves as a test and development driver for McLaren, also got some time in the MCL39 at Paul Ricard, continuing to provide him with a reference point for his simulator development work.

“I’m really excited to return to the MCL40 and do two more official Free Practice 1 sessions with the team,” said Fornaroli, who joined McLaren’s Driver Development Programme just under a year ago.

“The Mexico City and São Paulo Grands Prix are two great events, which will challenge me as a driver. Interlagos is a historic circuit with lots of mixed technical corners, and the altitude in Mexico City will definitely be a new physical challenge for me. It’s a great opportunity for my own development, and to also help the team over their weekend.

“This test at Circuit Paul Ricard was really beneficial. It’s been a few months since I was in an F1 car, so it was good to get back into it ahead of Mexico. This track is also really fun to drive, and of course driving the MCL39 for the first time made it even better. To drive a double championship-winning car was really cool.

“Thank you to the McLaren Mastercard Formula 1 Team for giving me these opportunities, and to everyone in the McLaren Driver Development Programme for their guidance and continued support. I look forward to being back with the team in Mexico.”

McLaren have also announced that Fornaroli will race for their new Hypercar team in the World Endurance Championship (including the 24 Hours of Le Mans) in 2027, while continuing in his F1 reserve driver role.

title: What time is the 2026 United States GP and how can I watch it?
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season marches on with this weekend’s United States Grand Prix, which will see teams and drivers face the captivating challenge of the Circuit of The Americas.

Max Verstappen took Red Bull to new heights as he finally won the Singapore Grand Prix on his 10th attempt, improving to P4 in the Drivers’ Championship in the process. His comeback might not be enough to topple Kimi Antonelli – who now leads by 102 points and could theoretically clinch the title in Austin – but once the Dutchman gets into a rhythm, he’s tough to beat.

Head to the RACE HUB or scroll down for more on how and when you can watch the action, along with the global start times for each session.

What time is the 2026 United States Grand Prix?

The weekend will kick off with Free Practice 1 at 1230 local time on Friday, 23 October, followed by Free Practice 2 later that day at 1600.

A final hour of practice will begin at 1230 on Saturday, 24 October, before Qualifying gets underway at 1600. The Grand Prix itself will take place at 1500 on Sunday, 25 October.

Check out the image below to find all the global start times for Sunday’s race.

How can I watch the 2026 United States Grand Prix?

You can enjoy coverage from every session live on F1 TV Pro (available in selected countries), which brings fans closer to the action via exclusive features like onboard cameras on all 22 of the drivers’ cars, and access to both Pre-Race and Post-Race Shows.

F1 TV Pro can be streamed easily via Apple TV, Chromecast Generation 2 and above, Android TV, Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Roku. F1 TV Pro is free of ad breaks and available with commentary in six languages.

Fans can also watch via F1 TV Premium, a premier service that invites fans to step into the heart of the action with the ability to watch races in 4K Ultra HD/HDR on up to six different devices, as well as a personalised Multiview feature available on select devices with 26 different feeds to choose from.

Viewers can watch every F1 Grand Prix, F1 Sprint, Qualifying and practice session live in 4K Ultra HD/HDR at home, with F2, F3, F1 ACADEMY and Porsche Supercup sessions also available to watch live on the platform.

Alternatively, live timing will be available on F1.com and the F1 app across every session during the Grand Prix weekend.

Where is the 2026 United States Grand Prix taking place?

The Circuit of The Americas was officially opened in October 2012, with the 1978 World Champion Mario Andretti given the honour of completing the maiden lap in his title-winning Lotus 79.

It held its first Grand Prix just under a month later and Lewis Hamilton secured his last win for McLaren in front of a bustling crowd, establishing COTA as another enticing modern venue that quickly won fans over.

From the renowned Texan hospitality to the medley of corners borrowed from other tracks – watch out for the Maggotts/Becketts-esque run between Turns 3 and 6, and a replica of Hockenheim’s stadium section at Turns 12 through 15 – every aspect of COTA is full of character.

What is the weather forecast in the United States?

It’s expected to be a warm weekend in Austin, with temperatures peaking at 28 Celsius. There’s also a very low likelihood of rain, which should make it a comfortable event for drivers and fans alike.

When can I watch F1 ACADEMY during the 2026 United States Grand Prix weekend?

After a two-month break, F1 ACADEMY returns to COTA for the first time since 2023 for the penultimate round of the season, with Red Bull’s Alisha Palmowski looking to further extend her lead at the top of the standings.

A three-race format will be in place for the second time this year and will feature drivers tackling an Opening Race, Reverse Grid Race and Feature Race, delivering even more action as well as opportunities to score big.

Free Practice will start at 1225 local time on Thursday, 22 October before an all-important Qualifying session at 1630. The Opening Race, which uses drivers’ second-fastest Qualifying time to set the grid, will follow on Friday, 23 October at 1750, with the Reverse Grid Race taking place the next day at 1800.

Last but not least, the Feature Race will round out the weekend at 1200 on Sunday, 25 October.

title: 5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the United States GP
excerpt:
After a weekend off it’s time to get another triple header of races underway, and for the next leg we’re heading across the Atlantic Ocean to the United States. A new Drivers’ Champion could be crowned, but there are plenty of other exciting storylines as the paddock prepares to return to Austin for what is always a big weekend.

Antonelli’s first chance to become champion

It’s quite remarkable that Kimi Antonelli finds himself in this position in just his second season in Formula 1, but such has been his consistent form, the Italian could wrap up his first Drivers’ Championship as early as this weekend.

The permutations are simple when it comes to what Antonelli needs to do himself, and that’s win the race. Anything other than victory at Circuit of The Americas and the title celebrations will remain on hold for at least one more week, but if he is standing on the top step on Sunday afternoon then he will also need some other results to go his way.

Team mate George Russell is Antonelli’s nearest challenger, and the gap at present means Russell would need to finish no higher than ninth for Antonelli to become champion should he win. But even then there needs to be another result that goes in Antonelli’s favour, with Lewis Hamilton - currently third in the championship - coming home no higher than fifth in the United States Grand Prix.

It’s a long shot for it all to come together, but stranger things have happened.

Can Red Bull and Verstappen keep winning?

Antonelli acknowledged the recent form from Max Verstappen would make for a “very, very scary” scenario if the four-time World Champion was closer to him in the standings.

Verstappen has won each of the last two races – the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia as well as the Singapore Grand Prix – while also winning the Sprint in Singapore to secure a clean sweep. Add that to a tight second place in Baku, and Verstappen was just seven points away from a maximum score over the previous triple header.

The top 10 driver/team combination wins in F1 history

That run has lifted Verstappen up to fourth in the Drivers’ Championship, but at 119 points adrift he has to ensure Antonelli doesn’t outscore him by six points or more in order to keep his own extremely slim hopes alive.

What was impressive about the recent set of results is that they came on a variety of different tracks, including ones that Red Bull have been successful on in the past, but also ones where Verstappen had never won. The question now is whether that all-round performance can continue into the next set of races, making Verstappen a factor in the fight for victory at every round.

Upgrades still on the horizon

Despite his wins, one of the reasons Verstappen was not fully convinced he will be in the mix at the front for the remainder of the season is the development race.

2026 has seen a hugely exciting rate of development with the new cars, to such an extent that there have been major fluctuations in form at the front of the field. While Mercedes started off with a dominant car, Ferrari took the fight to them at the start of the European season, and then McLaren came on strong with a run of two wins and three pole positions in four races through late summer.

Now it is Red Bull’s turn to be the biggest threat, but will it remain that way? McLaren are planning on introducing further upgrades in Austin to build on a package that was brought to Baku, while other teams are also expected to continue developing their cars.

That’s because there is a lot to be learned for 2027 as well, and if a team have space in the budget cap to bring the developments to the car then they can get a clearer direction on where they are heading into next season.

Mercedes have not stated there will be new parts on their car in the United States, but they are looking forward to a race weekend with three practice sessions in which to try and understand the upgrade brought to Malaysia, after struggling to get the full performance out of it over the past two rounds.

The newest rookie on the F1 grid

Even without racing for a week, there has still been some big news coming out from one of the teams as Haas confirmed the latest addition to their driver line-up.

Formula 2 championship leader Rafael Camara will join Haas next year – agreeing a multi-year deal according to the team’s announcement – and is expected to form a partnership with Ollie Bearman in 2027. Camara has been hugely impressive in the junior categories, fighting with Antonelli in the Formula Regional European Championship in 2023, winning that title in 2024 and then following up with the Formula 3 crown a year later.

Camara on the 'crazy' achievement of joining Haas in 2027

An impressive outing during a testing of previous car (TPC) event in Portimao this summer sealed the deal for Camara, who has yet to appear during an FP1 session but showed the adaptability required to convince Haas he was the best candidate for the seat. He beat high quality opposition in the likes of Leonardo Fornaroli, Ryo Hirakawa and Jack Doohan to the drive, and will get his chance to show what he can do in a race seat next year.

With Haas Team Principal Ayao Komatsu suggesting it is a formality that Bearman is confirmed for another year, the news only leaves Racing Bulls with an official vacancy, as Alan Permane’s team have yet to confirm either of their drivers for 2027.

A huge crowd at a driver favourite

Almost every race weekend can be classified as a big event given the number of sell-out crowds seen this season, but a trip to Circuit of The Americas has regularly delivered one of the biggest attendances of the year in recent times.

Austin is a city that attracts a massive number of fans to join the party, with activations all across town to ensure there’s no chance of missing the fact that the race is happening. And it’s often an exciting race, with the track layout an all-round test for drivers, including significant elevation at Turn 1, high-speed changes of direction through the first sector, and good overtaking opportunities.

Strategy is not always clear-cut, either, so we’ve had a number of tense finishes in recent years as drivers converge late in the race.

And while we’ll celebrate the size of the visit to Texas this weekend, it will also provide the first opportunity to get the drivers’ reactions to the latest addition to the F1 calendar, following the announcement of the African Grand Prix in Rwanda last week.

title: F1 to reverse contentious rule change after only one season
excerpt:
Formula 1 has shortened grand prix distances for the 2027 season as a result of changes to the power units, but the new FIA regulations —which were recently published — already stipulate that this will be reversed in 2028.

Formula 1's reduced grand prix race distance, introduced for 2027 to accommodate a major change to the power unit regulations, will only last a single season.

From 2028, the standard race distance will revert to its previous length, 305 kilometres, the FIA has confirmed after the decision to cut it to 290 kilometres as a temporary measure next year.

The FIA and Formula 1 have agreed to further adjust the balance between the internal combustion engine and the electric motor from 2027, following criticism of the current power unit regulations.

Under the 2026 rules, the combustion engine and the electrical system provide 53 and 47 per cent of total power respectively. That split will shift to 58/42 from 2027, before a 60/40 ratio is targeted for 2028.

But what effect does that have on race distances?

The change means the power units become more reliant on the combustion engine once again.

To boost output from that side of the unit, the permitted fuel flow is also being increased, which allows the cars to burn more fuel during a grand prix.

To cover the same race distance, teams could therefore need larger fuel tanks. That may require changes to the chassis, bringing extra development work and cost with it.

To limit those complications for 2027, the standard race distance is being cut from 305 to 290 kilometres. That way, teams will not need to make immediate, far-reaching changes to their cars to accommodate the higher fuel requirement.

Monaco remains the exception, with its race distance staying at 260 kilometres.

Just a one-year fix

Notably, the FIA has already written changes for the 2028 season into the 2027 regulations, which were recently published after the latest meeting of the World Motor Sport Council (WMSC).

Article B2.5.2 states that the standard race distance will return to 305 kilometres from that year, coinciding with the next step in the power unit rules, when the combustion engine-to-electric motor ratio moves further towards 60/40, and the fuel flow limit is raised again.

In other words, the shorter races due to arrive in 2027 are not a lasting fix but a stopgap, buying teams time before they have to confront the bigger packaging challenge that comes with the final step of the power unit shake-up.

The return to the longer race distance raises the question of how teams will handle the extra fuel requirement from 2028 onwards.

The regulation change itself does not confirm which technical solutions will be chosen, or what adjustments teams will ultimately make to their chassis.

title: Court case breaks out in Texas ahead of United States Grand Prix
excerpt:
A dispute regarding the design of the fuel flow meters used by Formula 1 cars has broken out in Texas ahead of the United States Grand Prix - with a lawsuit lodged in court.

Sentronics Holdings Ltd, a British company, has filed a federal lawsuit in the US District Court for the Western District of Texas against Allengra GmbH, a German market rival, alleging that Allengra has infringed its patent in the United States, which covers Sentronics right to be known as the inventors of a fuel flow meter which uses phase-modulated ultrasonic signals through a fluid path.

The patent, number 11,391.609 was applied for in April 2017, with the US Patent Office issuing it on July 19th, 2022.

That same month, Allengra revealed its own fuel flow meter, with the two companies then going head-to-head when the FIA opened up its tender processes to be the exclusive fuel flow meter supplier to every F1 team in 2023.

Allengra ultimately won the contract for the 2026-2030 period, but Sentronics has now claimed that Allengra is infringing its patent by using the same phase-modulation technology.

Sentronics has lodged the federal lawsuit in court, and is seeking damages and rulings against Allengra, and has demanded a trial by jury.

In the filings, seen by RacingNews365, Sentronics alleges that its own lab testing in 2024 proved that Allengra's system is using its patented design, and that despite being "on notice" of the potential patent infringement since August 2025 "when Sentronics served formal written notice of the infringement, Allengra’s continued infringement of the ‘609 Patent in the United States is therefore willful."

In a further claim, Sentronics's filings allege that Allengra has used the pedigree of an F1 tender to earn further contracts and relationships in other key markets.

Sentronics is not seeking to prohibit the use of the Allengra fuel flow meters at this weekend's Austin race, which will go ahead unaffected unless the immediate step of an emergency temporary restraining order is issued - something that is not currently being sought by Sentronics at this stage.

Instead, it is seeking financial compensation for lost profits dating back to the July 2022 issuance of its patent.

RacingNews365 has reached out to both the FIA and Allengra with a request for comment.

title: Max Verstappen clarifies stance on F1 racing in Middle East with clear message
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has moved to clarify his position on F1's planned season finale in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, insisting he never said he refused to race there despite his earlier warnings over the regional conflict.

The four-time F1 drivers' champion caused a stir in late September when he told Viaplay that F1 "shouldn't go" to the Middle East if neighbouring countries remained in conflict, regardless of existing contracts.

That intervention came amid a turbulent year for the championship in the region, with the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix already cancelled and the Bahrain round shifted to Sepang in October, from its original April slot.

Tensions have continued since the war first broke out in March — just a week before the F1 curtain raiser in Melbourne — with recent strikes against Iran and Houthi missile attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including King Khalid International Airport and Aramco's headquarters, fuelling fresh safety concerns.

Formula 1 has kept Imola on standby as a possible replacement finale on 6 December, though organisers in Abu Dhabi and Qatar insist the races remain on as scheduled.

Asked whether his earlier comments meant he could consider boycotting the two rounds, Verstappen pushed back on the suggestion.

"I said that I didn't want to race there? I just said that I love going there, but, of course, under the right terms," Verstappen told media, including RacingNews365.

"But I trust that F1 and then the FIA will take the right decision because they will have more information than us, and that's what we rely on."

Asked directly if that ruled out a boycott, Verstappen replied: "Like I said, I trust that they make the right call."

It echoes the sentiment of his original Viaplay remarks, in which he stressed the decision sat above the drivers.

"Normally I am happy to go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but you know, when there is a war nearby, and if some of the countries are in conflict with each other, then I think we shouldn't go.

"Then, it doesn't matter if you have a contract or not, I think. But it's not up to me," he said at the time.

title: Verstappen-Norris fight fundamentally alters F1 as Ferrari hit milestone for latest time
excerpt:
Max Verstappen and Lando Norris locked horns on this day, 20 October, two years ago, triggering changes in F1, whilst Ferrari wrapped up its 87th and most recent 1-2 finish.

Ferrari's most recent one-two finish, Charles Leclerc leading home Carlos Sainz at the 2024 United States Grand Prix, turns two years old today, and it remains the Scuderia's 87th such result in its history.

But the race is remembered less for the Scuderia up front than for what unfolded behind them, a clash between Max Verstappen and Lando Norris that reshaped how Formula 1 polices wheel-to-wheel racing.

Leclerc took the lead at Circuit of the Americas on the opening lap and was never seriously troubled, crossing the line eight-and-a-half seconds clear of his team-mate.

It completed a rare afternoon of Ferrari dominance in a season otherwise dominated by Red Bull and McLaren.

Yet the story of the day was Turn 12, where Norris attempted to pass Verstappen around the outside for third place in the closing laps.

The McLaren driver ran wide, rejoined ahead of the Red Bull, and held the position to the flag, setting up one of the most consequential stewards' decisions of the Verstappen-Norris title fight.

[Article continues below]

The ruling that followed

The stewards determined Norris had not been level with Verstappen at the apex, meaning he had lost the "right" to the corner under the Driving Standards Guidelines before running off track and rejoining in front.

"Car 4 was overtaking Car 1 on the outside, but was not level with Car 1 at the apex. Therefore, under the Driving Standards Guidelines, Car 4 had lost the 'right' to the corner," the stewards' document read via the FIA's official publication system.

"Accordingly, as Car 4 left the track and returned in front of Car 1, it is deemed to be a case of leaving the track and gaining a lasting advantage."

A five-second penalty followed, reduced from the guideline baseline of ten seconds because Norris had been forced wide by Verstappen's proximity. It dropped the Briton to fourth and promoted Verstappen to the final podium spot, widening the Dutchman's championship advantage at a critical stage of the title battle.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella was scathing in his assessment, arguing that the stewards had got it wrong.

"My view is that the way the stewards interfered with a beautiful piece of motorsport was inappropriate because both cars went off track, so both cars gained an advantage."

Norris himself stood by his approach, saying he believed Verstappen should have yielded.

"I mean, clearly I didn't give the position back because we thought we were in the right; clearly we weren't. I still think we were, considering Max went off the track; normally if you defend your position and you go off the track, you have to give the position up. In that case, I was ahead; I kept my position because he needed to give it back, and that's the way it is."

Red Bull saw no such ambiguity. Team principal Christian Horner called it black and white.

"So for us it was crystal clear that the pass had been made off the track. So, you know, he should have given the place back. He chose not to. So therefore there was a penalty. For us, it was very much a black-and-white scenario."

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

Guidelines rewritten over the winter

The row did not end in Austin. By the following weekend in Mexico City, multiple drivers had raised the ambiguity in the existing wording directly with the FIA, arguing it allowed a defending driver on the inside to release the brakes purely to claim the apex first, regardless of whether they stayed on circuit themselves.

An FIA spokesperson confirmed talks were underway.

"There was a general commitment to continue to update the driving standards guidelines. Bearing in mind the drivers requested the drivers' racing guidelines and agreed to their introduction along with the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, each time they are updated it is consultation with the drivers."

Discussions culminated at a further meeting during the Qatar Grand Prix weekend, where the GPDA and FIA agreed to defer formal rewrites until the new year. George Russell, present at those talks, described progress without divulging detail.

"It was pretty productive. I don't want to go into detail what was spoken about. But I think a lot of drivers are aligned that if you are the overtaking car on the inside, rule number one is you have to be..."

The revised Driving Standards Guidelines were published by the FIA in February 2025. They explicitly required an overtaking car on the inside to take a reasonable racing line and stay within track limits throughout a move, closing the apex-ownership loophole exposed at COTA.

Verstappen, for his part, framed the new era simply: "I think it's quite clear what is allowed and what isn't allowed, so I think everyone is adjusting to that... I don't know, for me it's always better to leave it more natural. But I just follow the rules."

title: Barcelona to fill looming F1 void as eye-catching contract signed - report
excerpt:
The Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya has signed an agreement to bring IndyCar to Europe after the success of Spain's Alex Palou, according to reports.

The former host track of the Spanish Grand Prix, Barcelona is set to enter a rotational period on the grand prix calendar along with the Belgian Grand Prix, with the Spanish race set to take place in even-numbered years from 2028 until 2032.

Having already lost the formal 'Spanish GP' title to the new Madrid in the capital, Barcelona was keen to fill the void with a high-profile championship - and, according to Motorsport.com, has penned a deal with IndyCar to bring the series to Europe for the first time ever.

The track also recently hosted the World Endurance Championship's Barcelona Six Hours.

Since the Indy Racing League ran first in 1996, the series has not raced in Europe, with events in North America, South America, Australia, and Japan, whilst the rival CART series did race in Europe until it eventually folded into the IRL to create what is known as IndyCar today.

The race is expected to feature in the second-half of the calendar, with IndyCar currently only having published its 2027 schedule for 10 rounds up to June 27th's trip to Road America.

The news comes after the astonishing success of Alex Palou, now a five-time series champion, who has established himself as one of the all-time greats since his debut in 2020.

In the seven full seasons Palou has completed in IndyCar, he has won five titles and in 2025, claimed his first oval victory, doing so in the Indianapolis 500.

Only A.J Foyt (seven) and former Ganassi team-mate Scott Dixon (six) have won more championships than Palou, who was born in Barcelona province in Catalonia.

title: Christian Horner and Red Bull withheld information from 'wrecking ball' Helmut Marko
excerpt:
Christian Horner has explained why Red Bull became 'selective' about the information which was discussed around "wrecking ball" Helmut Marko.

After Horner was appointed as Red Bull team principal in 2005, Marko was installed as 'advisor' for Red Bull GmbH - and effectively served as owner Dietrich Mateschitz's eyes and ears in the team and paddock.

Marko was never formally a member of Red Bull Racing, and cultivated a blunt, out-spoken character during his time with the team, which came to an end after he retired at the end of 2025 - months after Horner was sacked in July of that year, with Marko and Red Bull CEO of Corporate Projects Oliver Mintzlaff making the decision.

However, in his upcoming memoir Drive, Horner described Marko as a "complicated person" and revealed why the team started to withhold information from the Austrian during the formative years of the late 2000s, with Horner claiming that Marko would "claim credit" for the team's successes when reporting to Mateschitz, and "cast blame for the setbacks.

"From his position, Helmut treated insider information as currency, and he loved to spend it wildly, often without care," Horner wrote in his book, a copy of which has been read by RacingNews365.

"Helmut was becoming an increasingly unreliable ally. His media activities were equally frustrating because he happily shared insider information with platforms he favoured.

"This was a direct threat to our intellectual property, and a journalist only had to wave their microphone in front of Helmut for the floodgates to open, no matter how sensitive the material might have been.

"The team became exasperated, particularly Adrian [Newey] who grew more agitated with every leak.

"I raised the issue with Helmut many times and he always aruged his innocence and sometimes denied having spoken at all, even in those instances when he'd been quoted directly and on the record.

"Soon enough, we became very selective about the type of information that was discussed in his company."

[Article continues below].

Marko a "wrecking ball"

In mid-2008, David Coulthard was weighing up whether to retire from racing, as Red Bull had Sebastian Vettel waiting in the wings.

Coulthard eventually agreed with Horner to announce his retirement at the 2008 British GP, his home race, with Horner pressing Marko on the importance of letting Coulthard make the announcement and retire on his own terms.

However, a month before the Silverstone race, Horner recounts Coulthard telling him: "I think I've just been retired in a toilet," after Marko directly questioned him at a urinal, "because we're taking Vettel next year."

Horner recounts how he was "annoyed" and that "typically, Helmut had come in like a wrecking ball and crushed a delicate process."

title: Charles Leclerc points to 'raw' factor Ferrari lack compared to F1 rivals
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc believes Ferrari is just lacking "raw performance" in its F1 car compared to rivals, but is good at hitting the ground running at grands prix.

Ferrari's mid-season optimism about launching a title challenge in 2026 has faded, with the team not winning a grand prix since Leclerc's success in July's British Grand Prix.

Although the chassis is regarded as one of the strongest on the grid, the power unit is lacking behind the Mercedes and Red Bull designs, with a fresh design introduced at the Italian Grand Prix to combat the size of the turbo.

Ferrari opted for a smaller turbo to eliminate lag and produce excellent drivability, especially at slow speed, but at the cost of top-end straight-line speed.

The Scuderia has also had a trait of starting strongly in practice sessions before falling back when the engines are turned up - something Leclerc has also noticed.

"I'm not sure we are particularly good on Fridays," Leclerc began to tell media, including RacingNews365, about Ferrari's propensity to hit the ground running.

"I mean we are, but I believe it comes more from the engine modes that others are running, and once we come to qualifying, they just have something that we don't.

"In FP1, maybe we are slightly more competitive in comparison to our competitors that have something more for qualifying that we don't have at the moment.

"But one of our strengths as a team is straight from the get-go having a car with a good balance.

"I think our car is quite peaky, but I think we do a very good preparation before the weekend on the simulator. The correlation has been quite strong recently, which helps us to do the work on the simulator back at home, and then arrive at the track and have a strong car straight away and a car I feel comfortable with.

"So, I think it's more down to the preparation. It's not that if we design a very peaky car, then we can extract more out of it. The raw potential of the car is not at the level of our main competitors, but I don't think making it more peaky will be able to extract anything more.

"I think it's just the raw performance of the car where we are a bit down at the moment."

title: Exclusive: Red Bull reveal knife-edge battle as Max Verstappen confidence builds
excerpt:
Red Bull has revealed just how fine a line it has been walking with the RB22's set-up, with technical director Pierre Waché admitting the team has been wrestling with balance and ride quality over kerbs and bumps for much of the season, but that Max Verstappen is now feeling increasingly at home in the car heading into this weekend's United States Grand Prix.

Verstappen enters the next round at the Circuit of the Americas off the back of back-to-back wins in Malaysia and Singapore, having finished second in Baku before taking victory Sepang.

The Dutchman will be chasing a third consecutive win this weekend, a run that would mark a significant shift in momentum after a difficult middle part of the campaign.

Waché, speaking to RacingNews365, explained that finding the right compromise between low-speed traction and high-speed stability has been one of the trickiest problems the team has faced with the current generation of ground-effect cars.

Rebalancing the car for one phase of a corner often came at the expense of another, he said.

Asked whether recent gains in kerb riding and overall balance stemmed from Red Bull's upgrades or simply the RB22's inherent characteristics, Waché said: "No, it's a target to solve this problem. I'm not sure we solved it. We improved the situation in low speed.

"The main positive aspect is that we brought a strong upgrade in Miami, Austria and Baku, with a clear step forward in terms of improvements to achieve our goals, in terms of car behaviour and overall performance.

"The main benefit, the main aspect for us to improve, was not only low speed; it was an overall performance gain, an overall capacity of the car to be used by the driver.

"Because when we tried to rebalance the car before, it was a little bit on the edge. When you tried to rebalance high speed, then low speed was struggling, or vice versa."

Max Verstappen finding RB22 sweet spot

The Baku upgrade package, which included revisions to the floor, diffuser and sidepods, appears to have been the turning point.

Red Bull has continued to build on that foundation through Singapore, with Verstappen's recent results suggesting the RB22 is now a more predictable tool in his hands.

Waché insisted there remains more to come, but that the car's overall connection to the driver has improved markedly since the summer.

"Now the car is a lot more connected," added Waché. "That was our target for sure, and, yeah, we try to do an even better job on kerb riding and stuff. I think we're not perfect there, clearly, but we've improved.

"It's clearly not there yet. But Max likes the car now. If you ask him, he will not say the car is perfect. But I think with these regulations, it's a difficult problem, and I think we still have room to improve."

title: Lando Norris declares 'I don't care' position as major F1 admission made
excerpt:
Lando Norris has declared that he "does not care" what other people think of him as long as he proves to himself he is capable of performing in F1.

The reigning world champion has been vocal throughout his career about battles with mental health and a lack of self-confidence in his abilities, including early in his championship-winning year of 2025.

After poor qualifying performances in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, Norris declared that he was "useless" and didn't know how to drive a car, before a late-season rally to claim the title by just two points and fend off Max Verstappen's late charge.

However, Norris has grown in stature in 2026, but detailing his ongoing battles with himself, he declared that the only person he needs to prove anything to is himself.

"I don't know if it's pressure or if it's just the fact that I'm able to question myself less because I have the reassurance inside that I can achieve what I want to achieve," Norris reflected to media, including RacingNews365.

"So I don't know if it's pressure. It's not pressure. Like everyone's here because they expect me to do good things and to perform every weekend, as you should, and as the whole team should.

"But I've always been the person who has to prove things to myself before. Like, I don't care what other people can prove to me. I prefer that I can do it.

"I always found it hard to believe I'd be able to win a race in Formula 1 until I won a race in Formula 1.

"I always found it hard to believe I could win and have what it takes to win a world championship until I won a world championship."

[Article continues below].

Norris's performances

Norris has put together a strong body of work in 2026, with two excellent wins in Hungary and the Netherlands, whilst he arguably put in the lap of the season in Spain to steal pole position from Kimi Antonelli by 0.011s.

Only an unfortunately timed VSC deployment cost the Briton a third win in four races, as he further explained that "deep down" he has proven to himself he can deliver.

"So now it's more that I, deep down, have that reassurance within myself. I have confidence, and I have belief in myself," Norris added.

"It is something I wish I had previously, but it's just not how I'm wired or how I work necessarily. So it's not a pressure thing; it's more a confidence in ability."

title: Max Verstappen fires warning ahead of 2027 F1 calendar sprint changes
excerpt:
It does seem illogical of F1 to stage sprints where it is almost impossible to pass.

Max Verstappen has questioned the wisdom of staging a sprint race at a street circuit where overtaking is close to impossible.

Verstappen won Saturday's sprint in Singapore from pole position without a single serious passing move behind him.

Although the four-time F1 champion won his first race around the Marina Bay Street Circuit, the result did little to change his view of the format.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Verstappen said sprints should be reserved for venues where cars can actually race each other.

"We shouldn't host a sprint where you can't pass," said Verstappen.

"You have tracks where you can race and can overtake, but of course, in some places you cannot pass, and we are going to have sprints there also next year.

"I mean, I'm fine. I just do my thing, and then that's it, right? But it's not what I like."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

Verstappen highlights major problem

Verstappen pointed to the car's limited overtaking aids as the root of the issue at a track like Marina Bay.

"The track is great, but also the problem we have at the moment is with the overtake mode, it barely does anything here," he said.

"You don't really gain a lot on the straights. So that, and with how all the rules are at the moment, with our lovely batteries, it just doesn't do much.

"You can't even get super close or have a massive overspeed at the moment. So we need to have a longer straight, or more of a proper hairpin to overtake, but even with that, we also need a bigger delta on the straight."

title: Colton Herta set for US debut in latest Cadillac F1 practice outing
excerpt:
Colton Herta is to complete his fourth FP1 session for Cadillac, and drive an F1 car in the United States for the first time at this weekend's Austin GP.

The reserve driver, who had already enjoyed outings in Barcelona, Hungary, and Italy will deputise for Sergio Perez in FP1 at Austin for his latest outing.

He will be the first American to drive in an official F1 session in the United States since Logan Sargeant finished 10th for Williams in 2023, and scored his only F1 point.

Herta has pedigree at Austin, and won his first IndyCar race at the track back in 2019 for Harding Steinbrenner Racing, before a second win later in the year at Laguna Seca.

"Driving the MAC-26 in front of the American fans at COTA is going to be special," he said.

"I have great memories at this track – winning my first IndyCar race here back in 2019 was a huge moment in my career, so stepping into an F1 car on this layout feels like coming full circle.

"I’ve built up a good rhythm with the team through my previous FP1 runs in Barcelona, Budapest, and Monza, so my goal for Friday morning is straightforward: execute the test program cleanly, help the engineers gather good data on the setup, and hand the car back to Checo with some useful feedback to support the team for the rest of the weekend."

title: Christian Horner declares true Liam Lawson stance after Red Bull axe
excerpt:
Christian Horner has said that he was "uncomfortable" with Red Bull's decision to promote Liam Lawson to the senior team at the start of 2025.

Following the disintegration of Sergio Perez's form after the second half of 2024, he was dropped for '25, with New Zealander Lawson drafted in as the Mexican's replacement alongside Max Verstappen.

However, Lawson had never enjoyed an F1 pre-season or started a season, and had just 11 grands prix to his name; nor had he ever raced at Australia's Albert Park or China's Shanghai circuits, the first two races of the season.

In Melbourne, Lawson suffered an engine problem and missed most of FP3 and qualified 18th before spinning out during the treacherous conditions in the uber-tricky-to-drive RB21, something even Verstappen was struggling with.

Next time out in China, Lawson was 20th on the grid, before climbing to 12th in the race, but before the Japanese GP at Suzuka, the decision was taken to send Lawson back to Racing Bulls and to promote Yuki Tsunoda to the senior team.

After his confidence had been "smashed", in Horner's words, Lawson recovered at Racing Bulls to finish 14th in the standings, including a career-best fifth place in Azerbaijan.

Reflecting on the episode in his new memoir Drive, a copy of which has been read by RacingNews365, Horner describes how he was "uncomfortable" with the decision to promote Lawson in the first place.

"Helmut [Marko] has championed the promotion, but I felt uncomfortable. He was young and inexperienced, with only 11 Formula 1 races to his name, and we would be asking a huge amount from him, and meanwhile, Helmut was playing games.

"Before the final race of the [2024] season in Abu Dhabi, he had informed Liam that he would be driving for Red Bull because of his influence. When I challenged Helmut on this, he typically denied everything.

"The move back to Racing Bulls was tough for Liam. But he really shouldn't have been promoted in the first place."

title: Oscar Piastri has 'no magic answers' to solve crucial McLaren question
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri believes there are "no magic answers" to solve the issues McLaren is facing with its MCL40 F1 car this season.

The reigning constructors' champions are currently third in the standings in 2026, and are just seven points ahead of a resurgent Red Bull, having also lost ground on Ferrari in second place over recent races.

McLaren last delivered a big upgrade at the Hungarian GP in July, with this initially prompting an upturn in form as Lando Norris won in both Hungary and the Netherlands before being denied a third win in four races in Spain due to an unluckily timed virtual safety car.

However, across the recent triple-header, McLaren slipped back to fourth-fastest behind Red Bull, Mercedes, and Ferrari, with Norris being very vocal that the car was tricky to drive and required immense input to get it to do what the drivers required around a lap.

Team boss Andrea Stella has promised that fresh upgrades are coming at the back end of the season in a bid to increase learning for the 2027 MCL41 machine, but in terms of finding instant solutions for the rest of 2026, Piastri feels there are "no magic answers."

"I think in the short term, it's probably as good as it's going to get," Piastri told media, including RacingNews365.

"But naturally, when you start giving yourself evidence of being able to drive a bit differently and in ways that aren't that natural, they slowly become more natural.

"So I think Malaysia was another good step forward in terms of understanding what I need to do and not having to work quite so hard to get there, and getting there a little bit more intuitively and without as much effort, which is ultimately the place I want to get to in this part of the year.

"And to fundamentally bring the car a bit closer to where I would like it to be, I don't think we're going to have any magic answers this year.

"The cars themselves are very different. The tyres are quite different as well, so that's not going to change anytime soon."

[Article continues below].

Piastri's own improvement

Addressing his own upturn in performance after a poor season in which he has not claimed a podium in 14 races since third in the Miami GP, Piastri pointed to his pace at certain points of the recent races in Baku and Sepang as evidence he was slowly making the progress required.

"But I definitely feel like the last two weekends [in Azerbaijan and Sepang], on a personal level, I've been performing much better," he added.

"In Baku, for the first stint of the race, I was very strong. The middle stint in Malaysia was very strong.

"So I feel like on a personal level, I'm definitely making progress. But it's still not as comfortable as I would like."

title: Will Kimi Antonelli win the F1 title in the United States GP?
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli heads to the United States Grand Prix in Austin this weekend with the opportunity to claim his first F1 world championship.

The Italian is 102 points clear of team-mate George Russell and 111 clear of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, with the magical number for Antonelli being a lead of 125 points after the weekend, when there will be just five races and 125 points left up for grabs.

For Antonelli to win the title in Austin, he must win the race for his part of the equation. If he does not win the United States GP, he cannot win the title in Austin.

Should Antonelli win, his lead over Russell would grow to 127 points and to 136 over Hamilton.

To keep their hopes alive, Russell would be required to finish eighth or higher and Hamilton fourth or higher if Antonelli wins.

If Antonelli wins, Russell is ninth or worse, and Hamilton is fifth or worse, the title will be Antonelli's - and crown him the youngest champion in F1 history.

If Antonelli's lead is exactly 125 points following the US Grand Prix, he will win the title on countback, as he will hold nine grand prix wins to Russell on three, who could then claim a maximum of eight should the Briton sweep the Mexico City, Sao Paulo, Las Vegas, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi races.

The number of wins is used as the first tiebreaker when championship points are level.
